detailed_summary: FusionQ introduces a fusion-based decoding framework for quantum error correction (QEC) that departs from the traditional monolithic or fixed-window decoding paradigm. Instead of constructing a global detector error model (DEM) or using predetermined temporal windows, FusionQ dynamically derives local decoding tasks from the observed syndrome. It builds open-boundary local DEMs around clusters of fired detectors and expands their footprints only when a local solution uses virtual boundary errors. The framework is backend-agnostic: the scheduler requires only a local solution and a boundary-use flag, allowing exact solvers, matching-style decoders, and heuristic decoders to be plugged in. A key theoretical result is a compositional optimality theorem: with an exact minimum-weight local backend and boundary-free publication, fusing the published local results yields a global most-likely error (MLE) solution of the original DEM. Empirically, with an exact backend, FusionQ matches the monolithic MLE result on every shot. Across different backends, FusionQ substantially reduces decoding latency by overlapping local decoding with hardware syndrome acquisition.

methodology_analysis: FusionQ's methodology centers on decomposing the global decoding problem into local subproblems defined by clusters of fired detectors. For each cluster, an open-boundary local DEM is constructed, meaning that errors can terminate at virtual boundaries rather than being forced to connect to other clusters. A local decoder solves each subproblem, returning a solution and a flag indicating whether virtual boundary errors were used. If boundary errors are used, the footprint is expanded to include neighboring detectors, and the process repeats until a boundary-free local solution is found. The published local solutions are then fused into a global correction. The scheduler is designed to be backend-agnostic, requiring only the local solution and the boundary-use flag, which enables the use of exact solvers, matching decoders on graphlike DEMs, and heuristic decoders. The theoretical foundation is a compositional optimality theorem that guarantees global MLE under exact local decoding and boundary-free publication. The approach also allows overlapping local decoding with hardware syndrome acquisition, reducing latency.
